title: Creating Interpretable Latent Spaces with Gradient Routing
primary_claim: Applying gradient routing to an MNIST variational autoencoder (masking all latent dimensions except the one corresponding to the image's label during training) produces a 10-dimensional latent space that specializes one dimension per digit, enabling digit classification via argmax over the encoding at 92.58% accuracy despite no explicit classification loss.
quote: we can classify digits to 92.58% accuracy by just taking the argmax over the encoding (which slider is the most positive), which I find pretty amazing.
metric: digit classification accuracy via argmax over latent encoding
tolerance_rationale: percentage metric: 5 points; post reported no spread, tolerance is a guess
blockers: vae.py's save/export section is hardcoded SAVE=False, which tries to load a 'vae.pth' checkpoint that is not committed to the repo (only the already-exported vae_encoder.onnx/vae_decoder.onnx are included) -- a re-runner must flip SAVE=True (or otherwise skip the load) to actually train fresh weights before the final eval block will work end-to-end
no requirements.txt/pyproject.toml; deps must be inferred from the import block
inspector_notes: Single flat script (train + ONNX export + eval, using # %% cell markers, no CLI) that is otherwise fully self-contained and trivially cheap to run; the gradient-routing mechanism is the `encode_and_mask` method that masks all latent dims except the label-selected one during the backward pass.
headline_artifact: final print statement in vae.py: 'Classification accuracy from encoding: {correct/total}', computed via argmax over the ONNX-exported encoder's mean output on the MNIST validation set
